meta.title: AI Skills Assessment
meta.euIntro: Providers and deployers of AI systems must take measures to support the AI literacy of their staff and others using AI systems on their behalf (Article 4). The Act does not require a certificate or any guaranteed level of literacy for an individual. Indicators marked EU AI Act show where the framework maps to AI Act obligations. Many of those obligations apply only to high-risk AI systems, and some fall on providers rather than deployers.
meta.verifiedAgainst: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, consolidated text as at 27 July 2026

domains.name: AI literacy & concepts
domains.desc: Understanding what AI is, how it works, and what it can and cannot do.

skills.t: Has not encountered AI in a professional context
No awareness of AI terminology or capabilities
Can define AI, machine learning, and generative AI in plain language
Aware of common AI tools (e.g. ChatGPT, Copilot)
Understands AI is used in the organisation
Aware of EU AI Act existence and that it creates obligations
Distinguishes between AI types (generative, predictive, classification)
Understands how AI systems are trained and what data they require
Can explain limitations: hallucinations, bias, lack of reasoning
Understands the AI Act's four risk levels: unacceptable (prohibited), high, transparency, and minimal or no risk
Can identify whether a tool they use may be high-risk under the Act
Evaluates AI system capabilities and limitations for specific use cases
Understands model behaviour, confidence scores, and uncertainty
Can explain AI outputs to non-technical stakeholders
Assesses AI tools against EU AI Act classification criteria
Contributes to AI system documentation and audit trails
Advises the organisation on AI capability roadmaps
Leads technical evaluations and proof-of-concepts
Translates complex AI concepts across all seniority levels
Leads the organisation's AI literacy measures under Article 4 and keeps internal records of them
Engages with regulators and standards bodies on AI governance

domains.name: Ethical & responsible AI
domains.desc: Ensuring AI is used fairly, transparently, and without causing harm.

skills.t: No awareness of AI ethics or potential harms
Has not considered bias, fairness, or accountability in AI
Aware that AI can produce biased or harmful outputs
Understands the concept of AI transparency
Aware of prohibited AI practices under Article 5 (e.g. social scoring, inferring emotions in the workplace or education outside medical and safety uses)
Identifies ethical risks in AI use cases within their function
Applies basic fairness checks before adopting AI tools
Raises concerns about AI outputs with appropriate parties
Knows when a fundamental rights impact assessment is required (Article 27: public bodies, private entities providing public services, and certain Annex III uses)
Avoids using banned AI practices; can recognise them in vendor tools
Conducts structured ethical reviews of AI proposals
Designs human oversight mechanisms for AI-assisted decisions
Champions inclusive AI design in their teams
Leads fundamental rights impact assessments where Article 27 applies
Assigns human oversight to people with the necessary competence, training and authority, who can override AI outputs (Article 26(2))
Sets organisational ethics policy for AI use
Embeds responsible AI principles into procurement and product design
External advocate for ethical AI standards
Accountable for avoiding prohibited practices (Article 5) and, for high-risk systems the organisation provides, for the risk management system (Article 9)
Interfaces with national competent authority on ethics and rights compliance

domains.name: AI tools & practical application
domains.desc: Using AI tools effectively and safely to deliver better outcomes.

skills.t: Has never used an AI tool in a work context
No ability to assess the output quality of AI systems
Has experimented with at least one AI tool (e.g. a generative AI assistant)
Can follow a prompt to generate basic content or analysis
Understands the need to verify AI outputs before use
Uses AI tools regularly and purposefully in day-to-day work
Writes effective prompts and iterates to improve output quality
Understands when AI is not the right tool
Critically reviews AI outputs for accuracy, bias, and relevance
Does not input personal, confidential, or regulated data into unauthorised AI tools
Selects and configures AI tools appropriate to a business problem
Evaluates vendor AI tools against organisational standards
Trains or coaches team members on safe AI tool use
Designs AI-assisted workflows with appropriate checkpoints
Oversees AI tool deployment and, for high-risk systems, keeps the logs under the organisation's control (Article 26(6))
Ensures staff overseeing high-risk systems have the competence and authority to override AI decisions (Article 26(2))
Defines organisational AI tool standards and approved tool catalogue
Leads build-vs-buy decisions for AI capabilities
Architects AI solutions aligned with strategic objectives
Ensures deployed AI tools are used in line with the provider's instructions and deployer obligations (Article 26), and asks vendors for evidence of conformity
Keeps documentation for high-risk systems: the provider's instructions for use (Article 13) for each tool deployed and, for systems the organisation provides, the technical documentation (Article 11)

domains.name: Data & privacy governance
domains.desc: Handling data responsibly in AI contexts, in line with GDPR and the EU AI Act.

skills.t: No awareness of data privacy in the context of AI
Does not consider data quality or provenance when using AI tools
Understands that AI systems require data and that data quality matters
Aware of GDPR and that personal data has special protections
Aware that EU AI Act has data governance requirements for high-risk systems
Does not feed personal or confidential data into unapproved AI tools
Understands the difference between training data and input data
Can identify when an AI use case may trigger a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)
Understands Article 10 data requirements: data sets relevant, sufficiently representative, as free of errors and complete as possible, and examined for bias
Knows that providers (Article 19) and deployers (Article 26(6)) of high-risk systems keep logs under their control for at least six months, unless other law such as data protection law says otherwise
Conducts or commissions DPIAs for AI use cases involving personal data
Defines data governance standards for AI projects
Monitors for data drift and degraded model performance
Ensures training datasets are documented and auditable
Implements data governance aligned with Article 10 for high-risk systems the organisation provides
Keeps, and can produce on request, the logs under the organisation's control (Articles 19 and 26(6))
Sets data strategy for AI across the organisation
Engages with DPA and regulators on AI data governance
Designs privacy-by-design frameworks for AI development
For high-risk systems the organisation provides, accountable for data governance (Article 10), record-keeping (Article 12) and the quality management system (Article 17)
Leads responses to regulator requests and, for systems the organisation provides, post-market monitoring (Article 72)

domains.name: Change leadership & AI strategy
domains.desc: Leading people and the organisation through AI-enabled change.

skills.t: No engagement with AI as a business or leadership topic
Has not considered how AI affects their team or function
Aware that AI is changing the nature of work
Can articulate basic opportunities and risks of AI for their function
Open to experimenting with AI tools in their role
Identifies AI opportunities and risks within their team
Engages team members in conversations about AI adoption
Manages concerns about AI job displacement constructively
Communicates AI Act obligations clearly to direct reports
Leads AI adoption initiatives within their function
Builds team capability through structured learning programmes
Designs change management plans for AI-enabled transformation
Measures and reports on AI adoption and outcomes
Ensures team members are supported with AI literacy measures suited to their role and context (Article 4)
Creates a culture of responsible AI use with clear escalation paths
Sponsors AI transformation at executive or board level
Builds AI into talent strategy, recruitment, and L&D frameworks
Creates organisation-wide AI culture and psychological safety
Accountable for the organisation's AI literacy measures under Article 4
Ensures governance, supervision, and oversight frameworks meet regulatory requirements

domains.name: AI application to organisational strategy
domains.desc: Connecting AI capability to organisational goals, strategy, and competitive advantage.

skills.t: No connection drawn between AI and organisational strategy
Has not considered AI in the context of business objectives
Understands that AI can contribute to organisational goals
Can name at least one strategic AI use case relevant to their sector
Aware of the competitive landscape around AI adoption
Links AI projects to specific KPIs or strategic outcomes in their area
Can articulate an AI value case to their manager
Prioritises AI initiatives based on strategic impact
Considers AI implications in functional planning
Develops AI roadmaps for their function aligned to strategy
Builds business cases for AI investment with measurable ROI
Integrates AI outcomes into performance frameworks
Identifies where AI creates or erodes competitive advantage
Ensures high-risk AI use cases are identified and assessed before deployment, ahead of the high-risk obligations (2 December 2027 for Annex III uses, 2 August 2028 for Annex I products)
Leads organisation-wide AI strategy development
Integrates AI into corporate strategy, governance, and risk frameworks
Engages board and investors on AI as a strategic asset
Benchmarks AI maturity against industry standards
Ensures organisation meets all EU AI Act deployer and provider obligations as strategy scales
Monitors changes to the Act and its application dates (already amended in 2026 by the Digital Omnibus) and adjusts strategy accordingly
